title: Why performance resists preservation (rev2)
content: A novel outlives its author because the marks on the page hold everything the work requires. A symphony survives because notation preserves the relations among pitches and durations that constitute the piece. Performance enjoys no such security. What a dancer achieves exists only while she achieves it, and the recording that remains stands to the event roughly as a photograph of a meal stands to its taste. This gap reaches well beyond the archive. Because a performance cannot be stored, it cannot readily be bought, sold, or accumulated, and therefore it sits awkwardly inside institutions organized around permanent collections. A museum can acquire an object; it cannot acquire an afternoon. Curators have responded by purchasing instructions rather than events, treating the choreographer's directions as the enduring work and each staging as a single instance. Yet this response imports the very assumption it was meant to avoid, since it relocates the work into a durable text and thereby denies that the passing encounter was the point. Some argue that the loss is itself the meaning. On their view a performance criticizes the market in art precisely by leaving nothing behind, and any attempt at preservation betrays it. Others reply that this romanticizes neglect and writes off whole traditions, above all those of communities whose practices were never written down. The quarrel is not merely academic, because it determines which histories can be told. Where the record is dismissed as false, the record thins, and later readers inherit an account assembled from whatever happened to endure. Loss, then, is never neutral. It distributes forgetting unevenly, along the same lines as who possessed time, money, and a camera.

title: Taste, distinction, and the shape of preference (rev2)
content: What we enjoy in music, food, and furniture feels deeply personal, and people defend such preferences as marks of who they are. Studies in sociology complicate this picture without quite refuting it. Large surveys find that taste tracks schooling and upbringing closely, and that the link holds even when income is held steady, which suggests that what people enjoy is bound to how they were formed rather than to what they can afford. The path proposed is one of habit rather than deliberate choice. Children absorb ways of paying attention from the homes they grow up in, learning which objects repay a long look and which conversations count as serious, and these habits later appear as preferences that seem to come from nowhere. Because they are acquired early and go unremarked, they feel natural, and their social origin stays hidden above all from those who hold them. Critics say the account explains too much. If every preference marks a place in a social order, then it cannot distinguish a judgment reached through long attention from one absorbed without thought, and it leaves no room for anyone to change their mind on the merits. Its defenders reply that the account maps tendencies rather than fates, and that showing where a taste began does not settle whether it is sound. The quarrel remains unsettled, yet it leaves one thing standing. Whatever else taste may be, it is not innocent of history, and the ease with which people report their preferences is a poor guide to where those preferences began.
